title: Profiling & Benchmarking ML Systems
interviewAnswer: I optimize only after measuring. I separate data loading, preprocessing, host-to-device transfer, model execution and postprocessing; warm up GPU kernels, synchronize correctly, and report latency distributions plus throughput rather than one timing number.
why: “The model is slow” can actually mean disk I/O, tokenization, CPU transforms or queueing. Bad benchmarks lead to expensive optimizations that change nothing.
intuition: Treat latency like a budget with line items. Measure each stage before deciding whether to change the model or infrastructure.
deepDive: GPU work is asynchronous, so naive wall-clock measurements can be misleading. Benchmark representative batch sizes and input shapes after warmup. Throughput and latency often trade off; p95/p99 expose tail behavior that averages hide.
workedExample: If a 200 ms request spends 130 ms decoding an image, 50 ms in the model and 20 ms elsewhere, TensorRT on the model cannot deliver a 5× end-to-end speedup.
commonMistakes: Timing one GPU inference without warmup/synchronization.
Optimizing FLOPs while ignoring data loading and serialization.
followUps: How do throughput and latency conflict?
What would you profile in a RAG pipeline?
production: Production performance tests should run in CI/load tests on representative hardware and track regressions by model/version.
